clue.text: Fish meat on the counter I spotted twice

indicators.note: counter means running against the usual direction, so the word for meat is read from right to left

blocks.note: ham is a cured meat
taken as written
surface padding: the I is seen, nothing more
the chunk built so far is written out a second time

explanation.surface: A fishmonger spots some fish lying on the counter, twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' looks like where the fish is displayed, but it tells you to turn the meat round.
explanation.definitionFit: The mahi-mahi, or dolphinfish, is a large tropical food fish of warm seas.

clue.text: Close to me, wanting a little peck, lips met to get working?

definitions.text: Close to me, wanting a little peck, lips met to get working?

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, so only the end of the next word is kept
wanting means lacking, so the following small piece is taken out of the letters it sits among
a little of a word is just its first letter, a small sample of it
letters that get working are set in motion and rearranged into something useful

blocks.note: the final letter of this short word
the opening letter of this word, to be removed
three words taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone close by, after a quick kiss, finds their lips meeting yours at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P from LIPSMETTO, add E, and rearrange to get MISTLETOE. Read whole, the clue also describes kissing under the mistletoe, so it is an all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistletoe is the Christmas sprig under which people traditionally steal a kiss, bringing lips together.

clue.text: BII, CAMRA, SPBW etc a help as to pub undergoing refurbishment?

indicators.note: a refurbishment rebuilds and rearranges, so these letters are reworked into a new order

blocks.note: five words taken as written

explanation.surface: Pub trade bodies are pictured helping a pub through its refit.
explanation.walkthrough: CAMRA is the Campaign for Real Ale, SPBW the Society for the Preservation of Beers from the Wood and BII the British Institute of Innkeeping: a jumble of initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Alphabet soup is the jocular name for a confusing mass of acronyms and initialisms, like these pub organisations.

clue.text: Barnet Fair following turning to hot fare

indicators.note: turning to means becoming, so one letter in the word changes into another

blocks.note: taken as written
F is the standard abbreviation for following
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
to do is to fare or get on, as in 'how do you do?'

explanation.surface: At Barnet Fair, a London horse fair, someone turns to hot food.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet Fair is Cockney rhyming slang for hair, so 'Barnet' alone means hair; the clue hides the definition inside the name of the fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnet is British slang for a person's hair or hairstyle, so a hairdo fits it.

clue.text: Unpleasant and cold round centre of Stockport

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one word wraps around the other
the centre of a word is its middle letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: icy means very cold
the fifth of the nine letters of this town's name

explanation.surface: Weather in Stockport, a town near Manchester, is described as nasty and chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: Icky is informal for sticky, distasteful or nasty, so it means unpleasant.

clue.text: A job to hold back horse, keeping its head turning away from the ordinary course

definitions.text: turning away from the ordinary course

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the word for restraining wraps around the letter
the head of a word is its first letter, and its points back to the animal just named

blocks.note: taken as written
a post is a job or position
in racing, to rope is to rein a horse in so that it does not win
the opening letter of this animal

explanation.surface: A stable job involves restraining a horse while it turns its head aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' does double duty: it is the animal being roped and the source of the letter. The definition is the dictionary wording for a speaker turning to address someone absent.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhetoric an apostrophe is a sudden digression in a speech to address an absent person or thing.

clue.text: Decorator, one taking great risks, has day off

indicators.note: off means removed, so the abbreviation for day is taken away from the word

blocks.note: a dicer, as in dicing with death, gambles dangerously
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A painter-decorator who lives dangerously takes a day off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decorator' suggests a house painter, but here it is someone who decorates cakes.
explanation.definitionFit: An icer covers and decorates cakes with icing, so is a decorator of a sort.

clue.text: Wham hit that sounds like Kiss?

indicators.note: something hit is knocked about, so the band's letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pop talk: is a Wham! hit like something by the rock band Kiss?
explanation.walkthrough: Wham! and Kiss are both bands, but 'Kiss' here is an ordinary smacker.
explanation.definitionFit: Mwah is an interjection imitating the smacking noise of a kiss, often an air kiss.

clue.text: Brand New Key singer’s good knocking out one medley

indicators.note: knocking out means displacing, so the new letter pushes out the old one and takes its place

blocks.note: the American singer Melanie had a 1971 hit with this song
G is the abbreviation for good
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A singer's good song knocks out a medley performance.
explanation.walkthrough: In MELANIE, G replaces I.
explanation.definitionFit: A melange is a mixture of varied things, which is what a medley is.

clue.text: Eagerly sought last of crumble in bowl

indicators.note: last of a word means only its final letter is used
in means placed inside, so the letter sits within the word for bowl

blocks.note: in the game of bowls a bowl is called a wood
the final letter of this pudding

explanation.surface: Someone hungrily wants the last bit of crumble left in the bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' looks like a dish, but it is the ball rolled in the game of bowls.
explanation.definitionFit: To woo is to court or pursue ardently, so wooed means pursued with eagerness.

clue.text: Having the power to expand summer month event am busy with it

indicators.note: busy letters are bustling about, so they are shuffled into a new arrangement

blocks.note: AUG is the short form of August
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An organiser's August event keeps growing as they get busy with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with it' joins IT to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Augmentative means tending or able to increase, enlarge or intensify something.

clue.text: Cope badly with sauce tasting of garlic?

indicators.note: badly means done wrongly, so these letters come out in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner struggles to cope with a sauce heavy on garlic.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is by example: the word covers onions and their relatives, garlic among them.
explanation.definitionFit: Cepaceous means having the smell or taste of onion, and garlic belongs to the same allium group.

clue.text: Veteran comic star’s lead role in Dad’s Army

indicators.note: a word's lead is its front letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of this word
Private Frank Pike is a character in the BBC sitcom about Britain's wartime Home Guard

explanation.surface: A veteran comedian plays the leading role in a revival of Dad's Army.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan, of The Goon Show, was a comedian who also served in the Second World War, so 'veteran' fits on both counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Spike Milligan was the war-veteran British comedian famous for The Goon Show and his surreal humour.

clue.text: Bistro worker omitting one element of recipe in pans is crying

indicators.note: omitting means leaving out, so one letter is dropped from the worker's title
in means placed inside, so the letter goes within the word for pans

blocks.note: a waiter works in a bistro
I is the Roman numeral for one
woks are Chinese frying pans
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on a prescription

explanation.surface: A bistro worker who left out an ingredient is now in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element of recipe' suggests an ingredient, but it means the abbreviation R. WAITER loses I; R goes into WOKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning on the waterworks is a colloquial idiom for shedding tears, so the waterworks means crying.

clue.text: Speech on dispatch box after end of debate

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, the only one used

blocks.note: the final letter of this word
a loge is a box in a theatre

explanation.surface: A minister speaks at the dispatch box in the Commons at the close of a debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispatch box' is the Commons lectern, but 'dispatch' here means killing: the speech honours someone dead.
explanation.definitionFit: An eloge is a funeral oration or formal eulogy delivered about someone who has died.

clue.text: Time when my right hand flipped gold coin

indicators.note: flipped means turned over end to end, so the run of words that follows time is read backwards

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
H is the abbreviation for hand

explanation.surface: A coin-tosser recalls the moment their right hand flipped a gold coin.
explanation.walkthrough: The time abbreviation stays at the front; only the words after it are turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: The thrymsa was a small Anglo-Saxon gold coin of the seventh century, a historical piece of money.

clue.text: Nice manager running surgeries?

indicators.note: running letters are in motion, so they are moved into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A practice manager is pictured running doctors' surgeries.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French city, flagging a French word, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A regisseur is a French stage manager or director, someone managing a production in Nice or elsewhere in France.

clue.text: Extrovert man, foremost of executives, put on board

indicators.note: foremost means first, so only the opening letter of the word is used

blocks.note: a lad is a lively, boisterous young man
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: An outgoing man, ahead of the other executives, is appointed to the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on board' suggests joining a company board, but it means loading cargo onto a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To lade is to load cargo or goods onto a ship or vehicle.

clue.text: Conference delegate two hours before midnight intensely scratching backside

indicators.note: scratching means striking out, and the backside of a word is its end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: two hours before midnight is at ten o'clock
deep can mean intensely, as in deeply felt

explanation.surface: A conference delegate, up late at ten, scratches their bottom intently.
explanation.walkthrough: AT TEN, then DEEP without its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An attendee is someone present at an event such as a conference, which a delegate is.

clue.text: Elaborating too much on idling around Easter on vacation

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the word for idling wraps about the kept letters
on vacation means emptied, so the middle of the word is cleared out, keeping only its outer letters

blocks.note: o' is a short dialect form of on, as in o' nights
vegging out is idling about lazily
just the first and last letters of this word

explanation.surface: Someone lazing around over the Easter holiday is making too much of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' wants to join the definition as 'elaborating on', but it supplies the opening letter. Vegging out is British slang for lazing.
explanation.definitionFit: To over-egg the pudding is an idiom for exaggerating or adding too much embellishment.

clue.text: Vicar left rear of vicarage catching what bus?

definitions.note: a bus is one example of a vehicle

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter, which is all that is used
catching means trapping inside, so the short word for vicar holds the word for what

blocks.note: Vic is short for vicar
eh? asks what? when you mishear
L is the abbreviation for left
its last letter

explanation.surface: A vicar left by the back of the vicarage, asking which bus to catch.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: a bus is only one kind of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus is a road vehicle carrying passengers, so it is one kind of vehicle.

clue.text: Home Office employee, translator, absorbing role with week off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so these letters are rearranged
absorbing means taking in, so the abbreviation surrounds the rearranged letters

blocks.note: TR is the abbreviation for translator
role and week taken as written

explanation.surface: A government translator in the Home Office takes on a role with a week's leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home Office' suggests the British government department; here it is an office at home. 'with' is part of the letters only as a joiner.
explanation.definitionFit: A teleworker works remotely from home using telecommunications, so their office is at home.

clue.text: Revolutionary look in tent — Scandinavian mat?

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the word for look sits within the word for tent
a revolution turns something right round, so the combined letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a gur is a tent, the Mongolian ger
a ray is a glance or look in old usage

explanation.surface: A radical new look is planned for the inside of a tent.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the tent and the look are obscure Chambers words, so this is one to build from the definition and crossers.
explanation.definitionFit: A rya rug is a traditional Scandinavian hand-woven rug with a deep, shaggy wool pile.

clue.text: Biting into hot chip welcomed some language!

indicators.note: biting into means taking a piece out of the middle, so the letters are found inside the following words

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning these three words

explanation.surface: Someone biting into a hot chip lets out some strong language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some language' suggests swearing at a burnt mouth, but it is a real language.
explanation.definitionFit: Otchipwe is another name for Ojibwa, the Algonquian tongue of a North American Indigenous people.

clue.text: Cockeyed Bob leaving on bike

indicators.note: leaving means departing from, so the next small word is taken away

blocks.note: cockeyed bob is Australian slang for a sudden violent storm
taken as written, to be removed

explanation.surface: A squint-eyed man called Bob sets off on a bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name, but cockeyed bob is a single Australian slang term for a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: As verbs, to bike and to cycle both mean to ride a bicycle.

clue.text: Baby hawk put back after opening of egg

indicators.note: back means backwards, so the word for put is read from right to left
the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of this word
to put something is to express or say it

explanation.surface: A hawk chick is put back in the nest after the egg opens.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyas is a young hawk taken from the nest for training in falconry.

clue.text: Favour returned for novice

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word for favour is read backwards

blocks.note: a boon is a favour or blessing

explanation.surface: A favour is repaid to a beginner.
explanation.definitionFit: Noob is gaming and internet slang for a newcomer or beginner, especially an inept one.

clue.text: Rodents run back into scattered trash

indicators.note: back means backwards, so the word for run is read from right to left
into means placed inside, so these letters go within the others
scattered letters are thrown about and come back in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
to run is to go

explanation.surface: Rats scurry back into some strewn rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The animal is the hutia of Cuba and the West Indies, which Chambers lists under this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hog rats are hutias, large Caribbean rodents, so the plural names a group of rodents.

clue.text: Perhaps reading poem Spenser’s way?

blocks.note: reading is one of the three Rs, the basics of education
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether reading poems is the way Spenser did it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that reading is an example of an R. Spenser was the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene, whose archaic spellings Chambers records.
explanation.definitionFit: Rode is Spenser's old spelling of road, a route or path, so it means a way.

clue.text: Plain face of canine cousin once taken aback

indicators.note: taken aback suggests being pulled backwards, so the joined letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: o' is a short form of of, as in o'clock
C stands for a canine tooth in dental notation
coz is an old word for cousin

explanation.surface: A dog's homely-faced cousin is startled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain face of canine' reads as an ugly dog, but the definition stops at 'face'.
explanation.definitionFit: A zocco is a socle, defined in Chambers as a plain face or plinth at the foot of a wall or column.

clue.text: Paisley’s dreary — colour lines evenly

indicators.note: evenly picks out the letters in the even-numbered positions: second, fourth and so on

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Paisley patterns are dull because their colour lines are evenly spaced.
explanation.walkthrough: Paisley is a town near Glasgow, so the definition asks for a Scots word, though it pretends to be the swirly pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: Oorie is a Scots adjective meaning dismal, dreary or eerie.

clue.text: Deck game with ring on deck abroad worked solidly

indicators.note: abroad means widely scattered or astray, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: bull is a game played on a ship's deck by throwing pads at a marked board
a ring is O-shaped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Passengers on a cruise ship play deck quoits overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a joiner: O follows BULL.
explanation.definitionFit: To bullock is Australian slang for to work tirelessly and hard, like a draught ox.

clue.text: Sharp-pointed steel topped tent

indicators.note: topped means having the top cut off, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a tepee is a conical tent

explanation.surface: A sharp steel spike stands at the top of a tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steel' is a poetic word for a sword.
explanation.definitionFit: An epee is a fencing sword with a narrow pointed blade, a weapon poetically called steel.

clue.text: Violent attacker is rolling, eg canned by lager?

indicators.note: rolling means turning over, so this short word is read backwards
canned by means put inside a can of the drink, so the letters sit within it

blocks.note: lager is a type of beer
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A violent drunk is rolling about after too much canned lager.
explanation.walkthrough: SIEG sits inside BEER, between its two Es.
explanation.definitionFit: A besieger surrounds a town with an army to force its surrender, an aggressive assailant.
